## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Abhiṇhajātaka* (Ja 27), translated by Bhikkhu Sujato under the title *Familiarity*, is a short narrative included in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing narrative, the Buddha delivered the discourse while residing at Jetavana in connection with the close companionship between a lay disciple (*upāsaka*) and an elderly monk (*mahallakathera*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The canonical verse begins with the words *Nālaṁ kabalaṁ padātave* ("No morsel can he eat") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The core story illustrates the platonic affection (*sineha*) formed between a royal elephant and a dog [Collins 2016]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the dog was reborn as the lay disciple, the elephant as the senior monk, and the wise minister (*amaccapaṇḍita*) as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877]. In the editio princeps by V. Fausböll, the jātaka appears as the seventh story of its section, directly preceding the *Nandivisālajātaka* [Fausböll 1877]. SuttaCentral records seven modern translations in five languages, including English [SuttaCentral].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any early cross-tradition parallels for this discourse [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus reports no Pali-internal text reuse and no cross-language matches with Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora at or above the standard similarity threshold [DharmaNexus].
